title: THE WOMAN, THE SERPENT, AND THE OFFSPRING: THE WAR THAT BEGAN IN EDEN AND EXPLODED IN REVELATION 12
paragraphs: THE WOMAN, THE SERPENT, AND THE OFFSPRING: THE WAR THAT BEGAN IN EDEN AND EXPLODED IN REVELATION 12

Before the serpent pursued the woman in Revelation, before the dragon stood ready to devour her Child, and before the cross stood on Calvary, God had already spoken a promise over humanity's darkest failure. What if the Bible's most terrifying conflict is also the story of the greatest love that ever came looking for you?
There is something deeply unsettling about the first question God asked fallen humanity.
“Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9, KJV).
Not because God had lost Adam.
But because Adam had lost the innocence of walking openly with God.
Imagine that moment.
The garden was still beautiful. The trees were still standing. The same God who had breathed life into dust was drawing near.
But something had changed.
For the first time, the sound of God's presence did not bring the comfort of fellowship.
It brought fear.
Adam hid.
Eve stood beneath the crushing weight of what had happened.
And somewhere in that garden was the serpent whose deception had helped turn paradise into a place of shame.
Perhaps you know something about hiding.

You can smile in photographs while carrying a secret that keeps you awake at night. You can sing in church while struggling with something you have never confessed. You can encourage everybody else to trust God while quietly wondering whether God could still want someone like you.
You know what Scripture says.
But you also know what you did.
And sometimes the distance between those two realities feels unbearable.
That is why what happened next in Eden matters more than many people realize.

Because before God drove humanity out of the garden, He announced a promise that would echo through the patriarchs, the prophets, Bethlehem, Calvary, the empty tomb, and finally the terrifying vision of Revelation 12.
A woman.
A serpent.
An offspring.
And a conflict that would reach its decisive turning point at the cross of Jesus Christ.
But here is what makes this story extraordinary.
The serpent heard the announcement of his defeat while the guilty humans were still standing in the wreckage of their disobedience.
Grace was already speaking in the place where sin had entered.
And the story was only beginning.
In Genesis 3:14–15, God pronounced judgment upon the serpent. At the heart of that judgment stood these words:
“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” (Genesis 3:15, KJV).
In Hebrew, the opening declaration is:
וְאֵיבָה אָשִׁית בֵּינְךָ וּבֵין הָאִשָּׁה
Ve'evah ashit beinekha uvein ha'ishah.
A close translation is:
“And I will put enmity between you and the woman.”
The Hebrew word אֵיבָה ('evah) means enmity or hostility. This is not a passing disagreement. It describes real opposition.
And notice who establishes it.
God says, “I will put.”
Humanity had listened to the serpent, but God would not allow the serpent's rebellion to have the final word over His creation.
The next Hebrew phrase carries the promise forward:
וּבֵין זַרְעֲךָ וּבֵין זַרְעָהּ
Uvein zar'akha uvein zar'ah.
“And between your offspring and her offspring.”
The word זֶרַע (zera') means seed or offspring. Depending on context, it can refer to descendants collectively or to a particular descendant.
That distinction matters.

Genesis 3:15 introduces a conflict extending beyond the immediate encounter in Eden. Yet within the wider biblical story, Christian interpretation sees that promise coming to its decisive fulfillment in one particular descendant: Jesus Christ.
The Hebrew continues:
הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ וְאַתָּה תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ עָקֵב
Hu yeshufkha rosh, ve'attah teshufennu 'aqev.
“He will strike you at the head, and you will strike him at the heel.”

The Hebrew verb shuf is uncommon, and translations differ between “bruise,” “strike,” and “crush.” The same verb appears in both clauses, so the difference in outcome should not be attributed to two different Hebrew verbs.
The contrast lies in the locations of the blows.
The head.
And the heel.
The promise portrays conflict and injury, but the image of a blow to the head points toward a decisive defeat.
Christian theology has long called Genesis 3:15 the protoevangelium, meaning the first announcement of the Gospel.
That term is theological, not a Hebrew word found in the verse. Genesis does not yet disclose the full details of Bethlehem, the crucifixion, or the resurrection.
But the unfolding canon reveals why Christians read this passage as the beginning of a promise fulfilled in Christ.
And consider where God spoke it.
Not in a sanctuary filled with worshipers.
Not among people celebrating their obedience.
But in the presence of people who had just disobeyed Him.
God's redemptive purpose was announced while humanity stood exposed.
That does not make sin harmless.
Adam and Eve still faced painful consequences. Death entered the human story. They were expelled from Eden.
Grace did not erase the seriousness of rebellion.
It revealed that rebellion would not be the final chapter.
And that is where this ancient story reaches into your life.
The enemy would have you believe that your worst decision is your permanent identity.
That your shame is stronger than God's mercy.
That because you fell, there can be no restoration.
But the God of Genesis 3 was already announcing His purpose to defeat evil before Adam and Eve could do anything to repair what they had broken.
They could not undo their disobedience.
They could not manufacture innocence.
They could not reopen the way to the tree of life.
They needed God to act.
And so do we.
But Genesis 3:15 does not stand alone.
Follow the promise through Scripture, and a pattern begins to emerge.
In Genesis 4, Eve gave birth to Cain and Abel. Yet the first family did not escape the devastation of sin. Cain murdered his brother, and the ground received innocent blood.
Then another son was born.
Seth.
Genesis 4:25 records Eve's recognition that God had appointed another offspring in place of Abel.
The promise continued through a wounded family.
Later, humanity's wickedness filled the earth, but God preserved Noah and his household through the flood.
After Babel, God called Abraham and promised that through his offspring the nations would receive blessing.
Genesis 22:18 declares:
“And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice.” (KJV).
The Hebrew word for offspring is again zera'.
Paul later draws attention to this promise in Galatians 3:16 and identifies Christ as its ultimate fulfillment.

This does not mean every occurrence of zera' in Genesis refers exclusively to one person. Abraham's offspring includes his descendants in its historical setting. Paul's inspired argument identifies the promised blessing as reaching its fulfillment in Christ.
The story moves forward.
Through Isaac.
Through Jacob.
Through Judah.
Through David.
Through generations marked by courage and cowardice, faith and failure, repentance and rebellion.
The biblical genealogies are not merely ancient lists of unfamiliar names.
They trace God's faithfulness through human history.
And when Matthew opens his Gospel, he identifies Jesus Christ as the son of David and the son of Abraham.
The promised King had come.
But look closely at the kind of family history Matthew records.
Judah and Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
David and the wife of Uriah.
Stories involving loss, outsider status, moral failure, courage, injustice, and unexpected mercy.
Not every person in these accounts was guilty of the wrong done to them. Scripture does not flatten victims and perpetrators into the same category.
But together these histories show that God's saving purpose moved through a deeply complicated human world.
A world very much like ours.
Some people come from families where faith was nurtured.
Others come from homes where betrayal was normal.
Some carry wounds they caused.
Others carry wounds they never deserved.
And many carry both.
Yet the arrival of Jesus demonstrates that God did not abandon His promise because human history was stained.
He entered that history.
Then, in the fullness of time, an angel came to a young woman named Mary.
Luke 1:31–33 announced that she would conceive a Son named Jesus, who would receive the throne of David and reign forever.
Mary asked how this would happen, since she was a virgin.
The angel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her.
This was not an ordinary conception.
The New Testament presents it as a miraculous act of God.
And the Son born of Mary was not merely another descendant hoping to overcome the serpent.
He was the eternal Son of God who had taken on true human nature.
John 1:14 says:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” (KJV).
Think about that.
The One through whom all things were made entered the world He had created.
The One who needed nothing accepted human weakness without sin.
The One who would conquer death came into a world where death seemed to rule everyone.
And He came through the birth of a child.
This is where the story of the woman and the serpent begins to sound strangely familiar.
Because another biblical scene describes a woman, a child, and an enemy determined to destroy Him.
But to see it, we must go to the final book of Scripture.
Revelation 12.
John writes:
She is pregnant, crying out in the pain of childbirth.
Then another sign appears.
A great red dragon.
Seven heads.
Ten horns.
Seven crowns upon his heads.
Its tail sweeps away a third of the stars of heaven.
And the dragon stands before the woman, waiting to devour her Child the moment He is born.
Read that image slowly.
A woman in labor.
A child about to be born.
An enemy waiting to destroy Him.
The scene is terrifying.
But John does not leave us guessing about the dragon's identity.
Revelation 12:9 identifies him as:
“That old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world.” (KJV).
That old serpent.
The wording deliberately brings the reader back toward the beginning of the biblical story.
The serpent of Genesis.
The dragon of Revelation.
The adversary is now named explicitly.
The Greek text reads:
ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος
Ho ophis ho archaios.
“The ancient serpent.”
The noun ὄφις (ophis) means serpent, and ἀρχαῖος (archaios) means ancient or belonging to an earlier time.
John identifies the dragon with the ancient deceiver.
The enemy who appeared in the opening chapters of Scripture is exposed in the Bible's final book.
And the conflict promised in Eden has reached an extraordinary moment.
But who is the woman?
This question deserves careful treatment because faithful Christians have understood the symbolism in different, sometimes overlapping ways.
Revelation is apocalyptic literature. It communicates truth through visions, symbols, and imagery drawn from the Old Testament.
The woman's sun, moon, and twelve stars recall Joseph's dream in Genesis 37:9–11, where heavenly bodies represent members of Jacob's family.
This connection strongly supports understanding the woman as representing the covenant people of God, particularly Israel, from whom the Messiah came according to His human ancestry.
The woman also has an unmistakable connection to Mary, because Mary literally gave birth to Jesus.

In Catholic interpretation, Mary receives particular attention as the woman, while the image also carries ecclesial meaning. Many Protestant interpreters emphasize faithful Israel and the continuing people of God.

The woman should not be reduced carelessly to a single ordinary individual when the vision extends beyond the birth of Christ to the persecution of those who keep God's commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
Revelation 12:17 makes that wider dimension explicit.
The woman is presented symbolically in a way that connects the Messiah's coming with the covenant community and the faithful who belong to God.
This is not a license to invent secret meanings.
It is an invitation to read Revelation through the Scriptures that came before it.
And the identity of the Child is clearer still.
Revelation 12:5 says:
“And she brought forth a man child, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron: and her child was caught up unto God, and to his throne.” (KJV).
The language of ruling the nations with a rod of iron comes from Psalm 2, a royal psalm that the New Testament applies to the Messiah.
Revelation 19:15 also uses this imagery for Christ.
The Child is Jesus.
The promised King.
The descendant of David.
The offspring through whom God's promises reach their fulfillment.
Revelation 12 compresses the story of His earthly coming and exaltation into a brief symbolic scene. It does not narrate every event of His life in chronological detail.
And that matters, because the dragon's attempt to devour the Child is part of a much larger conflict.
Consider the events surrounding Jesus' birth.
Herod heard that a king had been born and became troubled.
He sought the Child.
When his schemes failed, he ordered the killing of young boys in Bethlehem and its surrounding region, as Matthew 2 records.
Joseph was warned in a dream, and the family fled to Egypt.
Matthew presents these events as part of the Messiah's story, shaped by fulfillment of Scripture.
Revelation 12 does not explicitly identify Herod as the dragon, and we should not pretend that it does.
Yet Herod's murderous hostility illustrates the kind of opposition that the vision portrays on a cosmic scale.
The Child was threatened.
But God's purpose was not defeated.
Years passed.
The Child grew.
He walked among the sick, the forgotten, the religious, the rebellious, the grieving, and the ashamed.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He announced the kingdom of God.
He forgave sins.
And He called people to repent and believe the Gospel.
The serpent had deceived humanity into distrusting God.
Jesus revealed the Father's character through perfect obedience, truth, holiness, and sacrificial love.
Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed.
Where sin brought condemnation, Christ came to save.
Paul develops this contrast in Romans 5:12–21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49.
Jesus is the last Adam, the representative of a new humanity.
But His victory did not arrive in the way the world expected.
It came through a cross.
And for those watching, the cross looked like the end.
The crowd mocked.
The religious leaders sneered.
Soldiers divided His garments.
His followers scattered.
His body was wounded.
His hands were pierced.
His blood was shed.
And the One who had never sinned was crucified among sinners.
Imagine standing there.
You had heard Him speak of the kingdom.
You had seen His power.
You believed He was the promised One.
And now He was hanging on Roman wood.
What happened to the promise?
What happened to the King?
What happened to the offspring who would defeat the serpent?
Perhaps that is the question the enemy wanted everyone to ask.
Because what looked like defeat was the very place where Christ was accomplishing redemption.
Colossians 2:14–15 describes Christ's victory over hostile powers through the cross.
Hebrews 2:14 teaches that through death Jesus acted to destroy the power of the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil.
The Greek expression in Hebrews 2:14 includes:
καταργήσῃ τὸν τὸ κράτος ἔχοντα τοῦ θανάτου
Katargēsē ton to kratos echonta tou thanatou.
A close rendering is:
“That He might render powerless the one having the power of death.”
The verb καταργέω (katargeō) can mean to nullify, render ineffective, or bring to an end in a particular sense.
This is not a claim that Satan ceased to exist at Calvary.
Revelation itself portrays continued satanic hostility.
Rather, Christ's death and resurrection decisively broke the devil's claim to hold God's redeemed people under the tyranny of death.
The enemy could wound.
But he could not overthrow God's saving purpose.
The crucifixion was not a tragic accident that God struggled to overcome.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
John 10:18 records His declaration:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.” (KJV).
The serpent's opposition was real.
Human wickedness was real.
The suffering was real.
But Christ was not a helpless victim of forces greater than Himself.
He was the obedient Son, giving Himself for sinners according to the Father's saving purpose.
And then came the third day.
The tomb was empty.
Death had not held Him.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
The wounds of the crucifixion were not proof that the promise had failed.
They were wounds borne by the victorious Redeemer.
And now the words of Genesis 3:15 can be read in the light of the completed work of Christ.
The promised offspring had come.
The serpent had opposed Him.
Christ had suffered.
And through His death and resurrection, the decisive victory had been won.
But Revelation 12 reveals another truth.
The dragon does not respond to defeat with quiet surrender.
He responds with fury.
Revelation 12 describes war in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon and his angels.
The dragon is defeated and cast down.
John then hears a loud voice announcing salvation, strength, the kingdom of God, and the authority of His Christ.

The passage's symbolism and sequence have been interpreted differently among Christians, especially regarding the timing of Satan's expulsion and its relationship to Christ's exaltation and the church's experience.
Yet the central theological declaration is unmistakable.
The accuser is defeated by God's saving work through Christ.
Revelation 12:10 calls Satan:
“The accuser of our brethren.”
The Greek term is κατήγωρ (katēgōr), meaning accuser.
And suddenly this cosmic vision becomes painfully personal.
Because accusation is something many believers know.
Not every painful thought is a direct attack from Satan. Human memory, conscience, trauma, and emotional struggles also affect what we experience.
But Scripture clearly teaches that Satan accuses, deceives, and opposes God's people.
And accusations can sound terribly convincing when they contain pieces of your real history.
“You failed again.”
“You promised God you would change.”
“You know better.”
“You have disappointed everyone.”
“After what you did, how could you call yourself a Christian?”
Some accusations begin with facts.
But they end with a lie.
Because the Gospel never teaches that sin is imaginary.
It teaches that sin is so serious that Jesus Christ gave His life to redeem sinners.
And His mercy is so sufficient that repentant sinners can truly be forgiven.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV).
Not because their past was harmless.
Not because their repentance earned salvation.
Not because they successfully hid every failure.
But because they belong to Christ.
The blood of Jesus does what self-punishment never can.
It cleanses from sin.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
And Revelation 12:11 gives one of the most powerful declarations in the entire vision:
“And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.” (KJV).
In Greek, the first clause reads:
καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐνίκησαν αὐτὸν διὰ τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἀρνίου
Kai autoi enikēsan auton dia to haima tou arniou.
“And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb.”
The verb νικάω (nikaō) means to conquer or overcome.
And look at the foundation of their victory.
Not their popularity.
Not their wealth.
Not their perfect reputation.
Not the number of people who admired their faith.
The blood of the Lamb.
Their testimony mattered because it bore witness to the One who had redeemed them.
Their willingness to remain faithful even unto death showed that their allegiance to Jesus was greater than their fear.
This passage does not promise that Christians will escape all earthly suffering.
It shows that suffering and even martyrdom cannot ultimately cancel the victory Christ has secured.
And that is a truth some of us desperately need.
Because there are believers who have mistaken exhaustion for abandonment.
They have prayed for years over the same family member.
They have fought private temptations that nobody knows about.
They have buried people they loved.
They have watched marriages collapse.
They have endured injustice.
They have tried to obey God while everything around them seemed to be falling apart.
And somewhere along the way, they began to wonder whether the struggle itself meant God had forgotten them.
But Revelation 12 tells a different story.
The dragon's rage is not evidence that he has won.
His fury appears within a vision that announces his defeat.
Revelation 12:12 says he has great wrath because he knows that his time is short.
The enemy's remaining activity is serious.
But it is not ultimate.
His hostility has a limit.
Christ's kingdom does not.
And the chapter continues with the dragon pursuing the woman.
She is given protection in the wilderness.
The serpent pours water from his mouth like a flood.
The earth helps the woman.
Then the dragon turns his anger toward the rest of her offspring.
Revelation 12:17 describes them as those who keep God's commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus Christ.
There is the pattern again.
The woman.
The serpent.
The offspring.
The hostility first announced in Genesis is echoed in Revelation's portrayal of the conflict surrounding the Messiah and His people.
But we must understand this carefully.
Christians are not independent saviors who repeat Jesus' atoning work.
There is only one Lamb whose blood redeems.
Only one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, as 1 Timothy 2:5 declares.
Believers participate in His victory because they belong to Him.
Their endurance is the fruit of grace, not a second sacrifice that completes what the cross lacked.
And the church's calling is not to identify every opponent as a serpent or treat every disagreement as demonic warfare.
Ephesians 6:12 reminds believers that their ultimate struggle is not against flesh and blood.
People are not the enemy we have been commanded to hate.
They are neighbors we have been commanded to love, including those who oppose us.
The Gospel does not authorize cruelty in the name of spiritual warfare.
It calls us to stand firm in truth, righteousness, faith, salvation, God's Word, and prayer.
To resist evil without becoming evil.
To speak truth without abandoning love.
To proclaim Christ without pretending that human beings are beyond redemption.
And perhaps the most astonishing part of this entire biblical pattern is what it reveals about the heart of God.
The first woman stood in a garden after disobedience.
The promised offspring entered the world through a woman.
The dragon pursued the woman and her Child.
And the final vision announces the ultimate triumph of the Lamb.
But this is not merely a story about an ancient enemy.
It is a story about the God who refuses to abandon His redemptive purpose.
A God who keeps His promises across centuries.
A God who brings hope into families marked by failure.
A God who sends His Son into a world that rejects Him.
A Savior who carries sin to the cross.
A risen King who will bring evil to its final end.
And a people called to endure by His grace.
Maybe you have spent years believing your story is too scandalous to be redeemed.
Maybe your childhood left scars that still ache.
Maybe you are ashamed of the person you used to be.
Maybe you are still struggling with the consequences of decisions you wish you could reverse.
Maybe you know the language of faith but have not surrendered your life to Jesus Christ.
Or maybe you once walked closely with God, and somewhere along the way, your heart grew cold.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence will disappear when you repent.
It does not guarantee instant emotional healing or the immediate restoration of every broken relationship.
It does not say that forgiveness removes the need for accountability, restitution, or patient rebuilding of trust.
But it does proclaim something infinitely greater than denial.
Through Jesus Christ, guilty sinners can be forgiven.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The alienated can be reconciled to God.
The enslaved can begin walking in new obedience.
The ashamed can come into the light.
And those who belong to Christ have a future that death itself cannot destroy.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the scandal never happened.
But God providing redemption through the crucified and risen Jesus.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you recognize yourself in the hiding, the accusing, or the exhaustion, there is something you need to know.
You do not have to make yourself worthy before coming to Christ.
You come because you need His mercy.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV).
Come honestly.
Confess your sin.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, who died for sins and rose again.
Ask Him to teach you to follow Him.
And when you stumble, do not make hiding your home.
Return to the Savior.
The same Gospel that calls you to repentance also calls you to hope.
Because the final word over those who belong to Jesus is not the accusation of the serpent.
It is the saving authority of the risen Christ.
And the story does not end in Revelation 12.
The dragon still rages in the vision, but Revelation continues toward the final judgment of evil.
Revelation 20:10 portrays the devil's final defeat.
Revelation 21 announces a new heaven and a new earth.
God dwells with His people.
Death is no more.
Mourning, crying, and pain pass away.
And Revelation 22 brings us to something breathtaking.
The tree of life.
The very tree from which fallen humanity was barred in Genesis 3 appears again in the final vision of God's restored creation.
The Bible begins with humanity losing access to the tree of life.
It ends with God's redeemed people receiving life in His presence.
That is not a coincidence of storytelling.
It is part of the Bible's profound movement from creation, through fall and redemption, to new creation.
From a garden stained by disobedience to a renewed creation where the curse is no more.
From humanity hiding from God to His servants seeing His face.
From the serpent's deception to the Lamb's eternal triumph.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing the historical facts of what happened.
Not by calling evil good.
But by redeeming sinners, transforming lives, and securing a future that sin and death cannot finally steal.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
If Jesus has shown you mercy, who in your life still believes their past has made them unreachable?
A brother who has stopped attending church.
A daughter who thinks God hates her.
A friend who smiles publicly but is privately unraveling.
A husband who carries years of regret.
A mother who prays through tears.
Someone who has never truly understood why Jesus died.
Someone who believes Christianity is only for people who have their lives together.
They may not open a Bible today.
But they might read something you share.
They might pause over a sentence.
They might recognize their own pain in the story of Adam hiding.
They might discover that the Gospel is not about good people congratulating themselves.
It is about the holy God saving sinners through His Son.
Not to prove how spiritual you are.
Not to collect reactions.
But because someone within your reach may need to hear about Jesus.
And I want to invite you into a conversation deeper than a simple reaction.
If you have experienced the mercy of Christ, consider sharing a few words of your testimony. You do not need to disclose anything that would put your privacy, safety, or healing at risk.
Your testimony does not have to be dramatic to glorify Jesus.
Sometimes the most powerful words are simply, “I was lost, and Christ found me.”
Not because typing those words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But because honest testimony can encourage another person who is struggling to believe that restoration is possible.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want people to encounter more than an emotional moment online.
We want them to open Scripture.
To understand the Gospel.
To grow in prayer.
To recognize false teaching.
To repent where repentance is needed.
To find encouragement in suffering.
To be strengthened in biblical discipleship.
And to keep looking to Jesus Christ long after the emotions of a single article have faded.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for truth, including those who cannot afford to pay.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
I will tell you that supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful way to serve others and honor God when it is done willingly, wisely, and with the right heart.
Those products may be useful reminders of Scripture and opportunities to share encouragement, but they are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
People encountering biblical truth is.
Your prayers matter.
Your sharing helps the message travel.
And your faithfulness to Christ matters far more than any number on a screen.
Because this ministry is not about building an audience that worships a page.
It is about pointing people to the Savior who alone is worthy of worship.
And that brings us back to Eden.
Can you see Adam now?
Hiding among the trees.
Ashamed.
Afraid.
Unable to undo what he had done.
Can you hear the footsteps of the Lord?
Can you hear the question?
“Where art thou?”
Now look toward Calvary.
See the Son of God bearing sin.
Hear Him declare:
“It is finished.” (John 19:30, KJV).
In Greek:
Τετέλεσται
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
The verb expresses completion. In John's Gospel, Jesus is declaring the completion of the work entrusted to Him as He gives up His spirit.
It is not a magical word that erases every difficulty from a believer's life.
It is the declaration of the Savior who has fulfilled His mission through obedient, sacrificial death.
And now look toward the end of Revelation.
The serpent does not reign forever.
Death does not reign forever.
The curse does not reign forever.
The Lamb reigns.
The One who was crucified is alive.
The One who was rejected is enthroned.
The One who bore the sins of His people will bring them into everlasting fellowship with God.
So when the enemy reminds you of your past, do not pretend your sins never happened.
Remember the cross where Jesus paid for sin.
When shame tells you to hide, remember the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
When suffering tempts you to despair, remember that the dragon's rage is not greater than the Lamb's victory.
And when you wonder whether your life can still become a testimony of grace, remember the promise spoken in the ruins of Eden.
God had not finished His story.
And for those who belong to Christ, the final chapter is not written by the serpent.
It belongs to the Lamb.
The serpent may know the scandal of your past, but he cannot overturn the grace of the Savior who holds your eternity.
